1.title: Know pets and petcare work
1.intro: Petcare services help owners look after animals. Learn what pets need and what each service does.
pts: Name common services: walking, sitting, grooming, training, day care.
Describe five basic needs of a pet: food, water, rest, exercise, health care.
Explain the signs of a happy pet and a stressed pet.
List words: leash, vaccine record, crate, allergy, temperament.
Identify which of the five needs a client's pet meets poorly and which service helps.
Compare dog, cat and small-animal care by time per visit and special needs.
Ask an owner what a good day for their pet looks like and write it down.
1.ex: A dog needs a walk twice a day. A walker meets the owner, learns the dog's habits and writes them on a care card. Two walks of 30 minutes make 1 hour a day, or 7 hours a week.
1.act: Visit a local pet shop or shelter and interview one worker about the daily tasks.
1.std: Task: list services and pet needs. Condition: after one visit. Standard: five services and five needs correctly named.

2.title: Read animal behaviour and stay safe
2.intro: Safe work starts with reading the animal. Many bites happen when signs are missed.
pts: Describe warning signs: stiff body, pinned ears, growl, hiding, tail tucked.
Apply calm handling: slow moves, no cornering, let the animal sniff first.
Check the first-aid basics for pets and know the nearest emergency vet.
Explain why you never handle an animal you are not trained for.
Describe the signs of heat stress in a dog and the steps to cool it.
Apply the rule that a dog stays on a leash and a cat travels in a closed carrier.
Use voice and distance first if two dogs meet badly; never put a hand between them.
2.ex: A dog backs away and licks its lips when a stranger leans over it. This is stress. The walker steps back, speaks softly and lets the dog come closer. In ten minutes at the park, 2 of 5 dogs showed stress signs, which is 40%.
2.act: Watch ten minutes of dogs in a park. Write down five body signs and what each may mean.
2.std: Task: read animal signals. Condition: ten minutes of observation. Standard: five signs matched to likely feelings.

3.title: Follow the rules in Canada
3.intro: Animal and business rules are set by cities, provinces and the federal level. Always check with the local authority.
pts: Check local rules on dog licences, leash laws, noise and the number of animals at a home.
Explain that a home business may need a city business licence and zoning approval; check with your city.
Describe animal welfare laws: neglect and cruelty must be reported as the law asks.
Check the federal and destination rules for health papers before travelling with a pet across a border.
Ask your city whether a home-based pet service needs a business licence and write the answer.
Check whether day care or boarding needs a vaccine record under provincial or local rules.
Find the off-leash and park rules for your city.
3.ex: Rules table row: Dog licence | city | owner shows tag number | before the first walk | copy in client file. If the licence takes 10 business days and the first walk was planned for day 7, move the walk to day 10 or later.
3.act: Make a rules table for your city, with the official page and date for each row.
3.std: Task: list the rules for a petcare business. Condition: official pages only. Standard: each row has an enforcer, an action and a checked date.

4.title: Do the core care task well
4.intro: Pick one service and do it to a written method. Small, careful tasks build trust.
pts: Build a care card: feeding, medicine, habits, fears, vet contact, owner contact.
Apply a walk method: leash check, route, water, waste pickup, return and report.
Compare ways to do a task such as bathing or brushing and choose the safest.
Record each visit with time, what happened, and anything unusual.
Practice giving medicine exactly as the owner wrote it, only with written consent.
Measure walk time with a watch and compare it with the time on the visit note.
Check the house before leaving: door locked, gates closed, water bowl full.
4.ex: Visit note: arrived 4:00, walked 30 minutes, dog ate half its dinner, no limp, left water. The owner sees it by message that evening. Five practice visits of 30 minutes each take 5 x 30 = 150 minutes, or 2.5 hours.
4.act: Do five practice visits with a friend's pet and write a visit note for each.
4.std: Task: complete a care visit. Condition: with a care card and permission. Standard: all card items done and a note written the same day.

5.title: Price your service and plan your week
5.intro: A fair price covers your time, travel and costs. Many small sitters forget insurance and unpaid time.
pts: Compute cost per visit: time, travel, supplies, insurance, tax set-aside.
Compare local prices for ten similar services before you choose yours.
Build a weekly plan with travel time between visits.
Check what happens when you are sick: have a back-up person.
Calculate pay per hour by dividing margin by the hours of the visit plus travel.
Compare a fixed price with a price by visit length.
Set aside a share of margin for tax as a stated assumption and check it with the tax agency.
5.ex: Visit price 30 CAD, travel and supplies 5. Margin 25 per visit. With fixed costs of 400 a month, break-even is 400 / 25 = 16 visits. At 15 visits a week (60 a month), margin is 60 x 25 = 1,500, minus 400 leaves 1,100 before tax. Teaching numbers only.
5.act: Build a cost sheet and a weekly timetable for 15 visits.
5.std: Task: price a service. Condition: all costs counted. Standard: break-even visits are correct and shown with units.

6.title: Find clients and build trust
6.intro: Pet owners trust people who are clear, kind and reliable. Referrals matter most.
pts: Build a one-page offer: service, area, price, hours, what you do in an emergency.
Create a meet-and-greet routine: meet owner and pet before the first job.
Write a simple service agreement with cancellation, payment and emergency vet permission.
Track the funnel: enquiries, meetings, bookings, repeat clients.
Ask three pet owners what made them trust their last sitter.
Write what you say when a request is outside your skill, such as a sick or aggressive animal.
Collect a short written review from happy clients, with permission.
6.ex: Four weeks: 20 enquiries, 10 meetings (50%), 6 bookings (60%), 4 repeat (67%). The weakest step is enquiry to meeting; reply faster and test a short phone call.
6.act: Contact 20 people or local groups and book 5 meet-and-greets.
6.std: Task: win first clients. Condition: four weeks. Standard: funnel numbers recorded and a signed agreement for each booking.

7.title: Handle emergencies and protect everyone
7.intro: Plan for the bad day before it comes. A calm plan saves animals and trust.
pts: Write an emergency plan: who to call, nearest vet, how to get the pet there.
Check insurance options for business and animal care; ask a licensed adviser.
Apply keys and data safety: label keys by code, not address, and store them safely.
Explain how to handle a lost pet: search steps, notices, owner contact.
Identify the nearest 24-hour emergency vet and write the phone and route on the emergency sheet.
Check that the client signed permission for vet care before you take a pet.
Practice a calm report to the owner: what happened, what you did, what is next.
7.ex: Dog slips its collar at 4:10. Walker stays calm, calls the owner at 4:12, searches the area, posts a notice at 4:45, and finds the dog at 6:30, 2 hours 20 minutes later. An incident note is written the same day.
7.act: Write an emergency sheet and a one-page privacy note, and practice the lost-pet steps with a partner.
7.std: Task: respond to an incident. Condition: practice drill. Standard: owner called within minutes and a full incident note is written.

8.title: Run the service for real
8.intro: Now run the service for real with clients, records and a plan.
pts: Run a 60-day pilot with a stop rule agreed in advance.
Review weekly: visits, pay, complaints, pet health notes.
Create a 12-month plan with licences, insurance and growth steps.
Lead others: train a helper with your care card and visit note method.
Calculate visits per week and income per hour at the end of the pilot.
Compare results with the stop rule on the planned date and record the decision.
Identify one risk to fix before adding clients, such as travel time or one demanding pet.
8.ex: Stop rule: if fewer than 40 visits in 60 days, stop and write lessons. Result: 70 visits, which is 70 x 25 = 1,750 in margin, minus 800 fixed costs for two months = 950. Two repeat clients; add a helper in steps.
8.act: Run the pilot, write the review and present your plan to three people.
8.std: Task: run a petcare pilot. Condition: 60 days, real clients. Standard: results compared with the stop rule and rules re-checked with the city.

quiz: Name three petcare services.
Walking, sitting, grooming, training, day care (any three).
Name two signs of a stressed dog.
Pinned ears, tail tucked, hiding, growling, lip licking (any two).
Who sets dog licence rules?
Usually the city; check with the local authority.
What goes on a care card?
Feeding, medicine, habits, fears, vet and owner contacts.
Why do a meet-and-greet?
To meet the pet and owner and agree the plan before the first job.
How do you find break-even visits?
Fixed cost divided by margin per visit.
Why label keys by code?
So a lost key does not show the client's address.
What must be in a service agreement?
Cancellation, payment and emergency vet permission.
What do you do first in a lost-pet case?
Stay calm, call the owner and start the search plan.
What should you do if unsure about a rule?
Ask the city or a licensed adviser and keep the answer in writing.
